thread.title: America needs a common mission

author: Newsweek
title: America needs a common mission
text:
National identity is not created primarily through slogans. It is built through shared responsibility.
to see more of our trusted coverage when you search. In 1971, while I was a medical student at Walter Reed Army Medical Center, more than one Black soldier recovering from Vietnam looked at me and asked:"What are you—Black, white or what?
" I am Greek American and dark-complected. The question was not entirely unfamiliar. As a child on the Gulf Coast, I attended a segregated school, and my family was escorted out of restaurants because someone thought I might be mixed race. I told the soldier:"What difference does it make?
We are both soldiers, and I am your doctor. I am here to help you.
"More than half a century later, his question still resonates. As the United States marks the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, Americans are again asking, in different forms: Who are we? Who belongs? What do we owe one another?
What purpose, beyond individual advancement or political victory, binds us together? I have considered these questions throughout my life as a psychiatrist, Army physician and military commander. I was commissioned during the Vietnam War and retired as a brigadier general after nearly three decades of service. I treated soldiers, veterans and military families, led hospitals and medical teams, and served alongside Americans from almost every imaginable background.
Those experiences taught me that a national identity is not created primarily through slogans. It is built through shared responsibility. The United States does not need a new common enemy to recover its sense of national purpose. It needs a common mission.
One of the most practical ways to create that mission would be a universal system of national service that brings young Americans together across class, race, religion, geography and political affiliation. The psychoanalyst Erik Erikson argued that developing a coherent identity requires more than deciding how we wish to describe ourselves. Identity emerges through commitments—to values, relationships, work, institutions and communities. The comparison between an individual and a nation is necessarily imperfect.
But countries also require some shared understanding of their character and purpose. A nation needs a credible answer when its citizens ask what membership demands of them and why their common project matters. I have long been struck by a historical coincidence. Bill Clinton, George W. Bush and Donald Trump were all born in the summer of 1946.
I was born two years later. We came of age during the same period of extraordinary national turmoil: the struggle for civil rights, the Vietnam War, political assassinations, urban unrest and the violence surrounding the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago. Those events informed our generation's understanding of authority, patriotism, race, war and political power. Yet they did not teach everyone the same lesson.
Clinton, Bush and Trump went on to offer profoundly different visions of the country and its place in the world. That contrast is revealing. A shared historical experience does not automatically create a shared identity. National trauma can draw people together, but it can also leave them with conflicting memories, resentments and interpretations.
What matters is whether a society possesses institutions capable of turning experience into common purpose. Today, Americans are surrounded by institutions that sort rather than unite them. We increasingly live among people who share our educational background, income, cultural outlook and political views. Partisan media and social platforms reinforce those divisions, rewarding anger and caricature.
Even when citizens inhabit the same country, they may experience almost entirely different versions of it. The armed forces are not immune from America's prejudices and political conflicts. Military service did not eradicate discrimination, nor should it be romanticized. But it did something that has become increasingly rare.
It placed Americans from radically different circumstances in sustained contact and required them to depend upon one another. In military medicine, the mission was clear. Patients needed care. Medical teams had to function.
Soldiers expected to be judged by their performance and treated with dignity. People who might never have met in civilian life worked together because success, and sometimes survival, depended upon it. A system of universal national service should offer multiple pathways. Military service would be one option, but not the only one.
Young adults could serve in fields such as public health, disaster response, conservation or community development. Such a program could include pay, housing support where necessary, and meaningful educational or vocational benefits, along with accommodations for disability, caregiving obligations and genuine hardship. The precise duration and administrative structure are matters for public debate. The essential principle is that service should become a broadly shared civic expectation rather than an opportunity pursued only by those already inclined toward it.
Critics will reasonably object that the government should not compel young adults to surrender months of their lives. But citizenship has never consisted solely of rights without obligations. Americans already accept compulsory duties in limited circumstances, including taxation, jury service and, historically, military conscription. Voluntary programs already perform valuable work, but they tend to attract people from particular backgrounds and dispositions.
A universal program would be more likely to bring together young adults who would otherwise remain separated by geography, education, income and ideology. National service would not cure political extremism, inequality or racial conflict. It would not make Americans agree about immigration, abortion, guns, religion or foreign policy. Its purpose would be more modest and, perhaps, more important: to create opportunities for people who disagree to work beside one another toward an objective that neither could accomplish alone.
A durable American identity cannot be manufactured through ceremonial language or political marketing. It must be experienced. At 250, the United States remains an extraordinary experiment: a country that asks people of different races, faiths, histories and convictions to recognize one another as members of the same political community. That experiment cannot survive on constitutional principles alone, indispensable though they are.
It also requires habits of cooperation and bonds of affection. Those bonds are created when Americans meet one another not as stereotypes or political abstractions, but as colleagues, neighbors and partners in a common undertaking. America does not need to agree on everything. But it urgently needs something meaningful to do together.
Stephen N. Xenakis, M.D., is a retired U.S. Army brigadier general and psychiatrist who served nearly three decades on active duty.
